findings.summary: aReZonedCopySTILLMovesWhenTheOriginalAdvances re-zones to ZoneOffset.UTC -- the zone SimulatedClock.getZone() already returns -- so the one test written for the delegation half of the withZone fix cannot observe delegation. Every conformant implementation passes it, including the defect this commit exists to fix. MEASURED, twice, by running the suite: (1) with withZone restored to the pre-fix body `return this`, only withZoneReturnsACLOCKCarryingTheGivenZoneAndTheSAMETime fails -- this test passes green against the bug; (2) with the shape the JDK's own clocks use, `if (zone.equals(getZone())) return this; return Clock.fixed(instant(), zone);` -- a copy that SNAPSHOTS and therefore drifts, which is precisely what the row says must be impossible -- all four tests pass. So the assertion cannot go false for the reason it names, which is the pattern M4.19 deleted crossEpochOffsetsChecked() for. Fix is one identifier: re-zone to a non-UTC zone (Australia/Sydney is already imported in the file).
findings.failure_scenario: A later hand adds the conventional same-zone short-circuit to withZone and, for a different zone, returns Clock.fixed(instant(), zone). SimulatedClockTest stays green (verified by running it). A caller that re-zones the simulation clock then holds a clock frozen at construction time: LeaseManager reads the re-zoned view, never sees the TTL lapse, and every failover in the sweep silently becomes the polite-release path -- the exact 'two clocks that drift, one part of the run believes a lease expired and another does not' failure the javadoc at SimulatedClock.java:565-568 says the delegation exists to prevent, arriving with no test able to see it.

findings.summary: The 'WHAT IT DOES NOT DO YET' disclosure makes two claims and neither holds. (a) `LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest covers that at the unit level` -- it does not: that class has exactly one @Test, aLosingConcurrentAcquireCannotWipeTheWinnersBeliefOnTheSameInstance, which races two acquires of the LEASE key inside one LeaseManager. Two writers racing one CHAIN slot is covered by CommitLogSealWriteTest (sealingRedrivesPastADeltaTheOldLeaderWonRatherThanSurrenderingTheCluster, with its oldLeaderCommits helper) and by LocalSequencerTest via StealFirstPutStore. The pointer sends a reader to a test about a different key and a different race. (b) `carrying it into the simulation is M4.13's` -- M4.13's row owns the 1,000-seed sweep, delayed writes, reordered completions, partitioned leaders as an injectable fault and the withheld-write ambiguity, and says nothing about running pods concurrently; while FaultInjectingStore.java:144-154, committed in M4.12, instructs the opposite in as many words: 'THIS IS A NOTE TO M4.20 ... interleave them LOGICALLY, one call at a time from one thread, rather than one virtual thread per pod. Concurrency there would not corrupt the store, it would corrupt REPRODUCIBILITY'. So the deferral names a row that does not own it and asks for a thing the store in the same package says must never be done. This is the same defect the M4.20 row itself records having corrected once already ('an earlier draft deferred it to M4.16's two deferred progress assertions, and M4.16 contains no progress assertion').
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 is picked up from its row, which never mentions concurrency, so nobody carries the real-time slot race into the simulation; a reader auditing M4's completion condition reads this javadoc, follows it to LeaseManagerConcurrencyTest, finds a green test about the lease key and concludes the slot race is covered at both levels. The gap is then closed by nobody and looks closed to everybody -- and whoever DOES act on the sentence adds one virtual thread per pod and destroys the seed-replay property the whole harness rests on, which the FaultInjectingStore javadoc predicts and this one contradicts.

findings.summary: `scanTo = pods * rounds` is 3x wider than anything reachable, and the guard it feeds cannot fire and would be unsound if it could. At most one epoch is minted per round (one tryStart per round, in the leader == null branch), so epochs <= rounds < pods * rounds for pods > 1 -- MEASURED: highestEpoch averages 97 and peaks at 105 over seeds 0..29 at ROUGH, against 360 scanned, so 255 of 360 epochs per seed are scanned empty at 2 LISTs each (checkChain + hasChain), about 15,000 redundant LISTs per 30-seed sweep and two such sweeps in the file. Extrapolated to M4.13's 1,000 seeds that is still only ~5.6s of the <60s budget, so this is waste rather than a breach. Separately the guard probes exactly ONE epoch above the bound, and epochs are NOT contiguous with chains: a tryAcquire that mints epoch E followed by a start that throws before log.open leaves E with nothing under its log prefix (M4.16's row: 'every failed start burns one', 'ancestors skipped in RUNS rather than singly'). So the comment's claim 'THE SCAN BOUND IS ASSERTED, NOT ASSUMED' describes a proposition that cannot fail.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone tightens the bound to the true maximum (`rounds`) or raises rounds so a run reaches it. A failed start burns epoch scanTo+1 without writing a chain, the next taker opens scanTo+2 and commits into it; hasChain(scanTo + 1) is empty, the guard stays silent, and run() reports 'no violations' about a chain nobody read -- the anti-vacuity failure the comment claims to have closed, arriving through the hole the guard leaves.

findings.summary: The starved-seeds discriminator is sound and I verified it rather than taking it on trust: healthy starved == 1 on three separate runs (deterministic; MemoryBinStore is a ConcurrentSkipListMap so LIST order is stable, and nothing reads a wall clock), and with the lapse-advance removed starved == 5 and THIS assertion is the one that fails -- both throughput floors pass under the stall, exactly as the comment says. `the clean run's worst seed still makes 52` also checks out exactly (measured 52 over CLEAN seeds 0..29). What the comment does not say is how close the margin actually is: seed 14 makes 1 commit, seeds 6 and 7 make 2, seed 8 makes 3, so four seeds sit within two commits of starving while the bound tolerates only one more starved seed than measured. And for the next hand: the alternatives are WORSE, measured, so they should not be reached for -- aggregate epoch churn looks sharpest (highestEpoch sum 2910 healthy vs 275 stalled, 10x) but asserts a pathology, since M4.16's own candidate fix 'minting the epoch only after start succeeds' narrows epoch burn ~95% and would drive that sum to roughly the takeover count, turning an epoch floor red on a FIXED system -- the trap this file already names about zombieWrites; failed acquires give no signal at all (3223 healthy vs 3303 stalled); rounds-with-a-leader 300 vs 240 and takeovers 77 vs 57 are both weaker than 1-vs-5.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.17's renew tick or M4.16's fix lands and moves two of the four seeds that make 1-3 commits to zero. starved becomes 3, this test goes red, and the failure message says 'measured 1 healthy and 5 with the lapse-advance removed' -- which points the reader at a stall that did not happen. Recording the per-seed commit histogram (or the four near-starving seeds) in the comment is what makes that failure diagnosable instead of misleading.

findings.summary: At ROUGH the sweep spends almost all of its budget on leader STARTUP failing, and Result reports nothing that would show it. MEASURED by instrumenting a scratch copy of the driver over seeds 0..29 x 120 rounds (3,600 rounds): only 300 rounds had a leader at the top of the loop, 3,223 rounds ended with tryStart returning empty, and highestEpoch averages 97 -- i.e. ~92% of rounds are tryAcquire winning an epoch and then start throwing an injected fault, burning the epoch and releasing the lease. Consequences for what the new floor certifies: 208 commits across the range against 2,133 for the same seeds CLEAN (a 10x degradation), and zombieAttempts totals 15 with zombieWrites 7 -- so the fenced-writer path this file calls 'the ONLY thing that makes I5 reachable' fires in 0.4% of rounds. Nothing here is falsely claimed (the file discloses that heavy faulting degrades the cluster) but Result carries commits/takeovers/zombie counts and no measure of how many rounds were productive, which is the same 'say how much you examined' gap M4.22 opens against Invariants.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change makes LocalSequencer.start fail more readily -- an extra store read on the failover path, say. commits stays above the floor of 30 and takeovers above 30 purely from the seeds that still lead, starved stays under 3, and the sweep reports a healthy faulted range while the number of rounds that ever reach commit() has halved: the anti-vacuity floor cannot see it because the harness does not count it.

findings.summary: counts() always writes one run key, new RunKey(STREAM, 0), so every I2 check the sweep performs is over a single stream. The offset-inheritance map is therefore always size 1 and a per-key offset counter is indistinguishable from a global one. CommitLogTest covers two keys at the unit level, so the module is not blind -- but the simulation's I2 claim is narrower than its javadoc reads, and this is the harness the milestone points at for I2 under faults.
findings.failure_scenario: A refactor of CommitLog.commit assigns offsets from one counter per chain instead of one per RunKey. Every seed of this simulation still reports clean because there is only ever one RunKey in flight; the defect surfaces only in production, where two streams in one segment would have their offsets interleaved and I2 broken for both.

findings.summary: theSameSeedReplaysExactlySoAFailureIsAPermanentRegression compares commits, takeovers, highestEpoch and faults, but not violations() -- the one field the test's own name is about, since 'a failure is a permanent regression' means the VIOLATION list replays. Cheap to close: one more isEqualTo on b.violations().
findings.failure_scenario: The checker, or the driver's aggregation of it, becomes order- or identity-dependent (an ancestor walk that folds a HashMap, say, or a Violation detail string carrying an epoch discovered in iteration order). The replay test stays green because the four fields it compares are unaffected, and M4.13's pinned failing seeds start reporting a different violation list from run to run -- which is exactly the flake-versus-regression distinction this test exists to buy.

findings.summary: flushSeq is a fleet-global counter in both commit paths -- `commits` for leaders (line 186), `zombieWrites` for zombies (line 175) -- and neither advances on a failed attempt. CommitRequest's javadoc declares (podId, flushSeq) 'that node's own monotonic flush counter ... the idempotency key M4.10 will use to ignore a replay' and says the simulation drives many logical nodes through this seam 'so the ordering and idempotency arguments are proven at M4'. As driven, the key is neither per-pod nor unique. LocalSequencer discards flushSeq today, so nothing is wrong in the tree; the traffic is what is wrong. Fix is a Map<String, Long> keyed by pod, incremented on every ATTEMPT.
findings.failure_scenario: pod1 commits seg/40 at flushSeq 7, the write LANDS under an ambiguousPut and the response is lost, so the leader stands down without incrementing commits; pod1 re-acquires and commits seg/45 at flushSeq 7 again. When M4.10's dedup lands and reads the key this record declares, the second commit is dropped as a replay of the first -- so the harness meant to prove idempotency generates traffic that violates the key's stated uniqueness, and the first seed to exercise it reports a commit shortfall that looks like a protocol defect.
